visible.summary:
The region's documented contact point with trans-visitor risk is prison placement, which national law sets: under criminal-procedure code Article D248 a trans prisoner is held according to the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still marked male are placed in all-male facilities. An investigation published in January 2018 recorded exactly that near the region's principal city: Paola, shouted at and threatened by inmates during three days in a men's facility after a 2014 transfer, and — in the capital — Kara B., held under notorious conditions after a 2016 protest trial; the national detention inspector-general calls transgender detainees the group that suffers most in custody.

The inspector-general's May 2021 opinion, covering every place of deprivation of liberty in the state and built from some forty referrals since 2010, finds serious violations persisting: isolation by reason of trans status, untrained staff, and a 2016 depathologisation law never translated into prison rules. It recommends that detainees choose the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation and trans-only wings, and requires continuity of hormone and medical care — recommendations whose non-implementation is itself part of the documented picture for visitors who are detained anywhere in the state, including here.
visible.tangentialFactors: The far-right municipal pattern documented here targets LGBTQ pride events and organisations broadly rather than gender expression specifically, but cancellations and hollowed-out permits directly reduce safe public space for gender-nonconforming visitors and residents in affected communes.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed investigation posted 12 January 2018: under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities - the group that, per controller-general Adeline Hazan, 'suffers the most' in prison. Region-relevant case: Paola, transferred in 2014 to Lille's northern correctional facility, was met by detainees shouting 'We don't want any women here!', a fellow inmate tried to attack her with a knife and she spent two days in solitary confinement; Kara B. was held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 Paris protest trial; the Ministry of Justice counted 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

National detention-oversight opinion of 25 May 2021 (covering every place of deprivation of liberty; prepared from referrals received since 2010 concerning transgender detainees): assignment to establishments or wards (male or female) is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and search procedures for persons whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation. It recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, urges research funding, and faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules.

visible.summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident record survives in this region's sources; that absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence, not as evidence of local safety. The national framework documented in this record applies unchanged in every commune and department.

That framework is centred on custody. Under criminal-procedure code Article D248 a prisoner is placed by the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still legally marked male are held in all-male facilities; a January 2018 investigation records one such detainee three days in a men's facility near Lille amid inmate threats, and another held in notorious conditions after a 2016 protest trial in the capital. The national detention inspector-general's May 2021 opinion — covering every place of deprivation of liberty, built on some forty referrals since 2010 — finds serious violations persisting: isolation for trans status, untrained staff, and a 2016 depathologisation law never written into prison rules; it recommends that detainees choose the sex of search officers and ward, prohibits identity-based isolation, and requires continuity of medical care, and names transgender detainees as the group that suffers most in the state's custody.
visible.tangentialFactors: The Béziers Pride cancellation is an anti-Pride hostility event affecting the whole local LGBTQIA+ community rather than gender expression specifically, but it removes the region's public visibility event and signals a hostile municipal climate that gender-nonconforming visitors would encounter in daily interactions.

sources.claim: National-framework investigation (BuzzFeed, Rozenn Le Carboulec, published January 2018) on trans women in French prisons — the custody framework the record applies unchanged to this region: Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code places detainees by the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still legally marked male are held in all-male facilities; a trans woman from Argentina whose passport lists her as female spent three days in a men's facility in Lille amid inmate threats (an inmate tried to attack her with a knife), and another detainee was held after a 2016 Paris protest trial; as of 1 November 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees in France, and damages obtained for one detainee's detention conditions were a symbolic 2,000 euros. No Occitanie-specific event appears; the article supports the record's claim that this national custody framework applies in every department.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 by the national detention inspector-general (CGLPL), covering every place of deprivation of liberty and relevant to this region because its visits included the Toulouse-Seysses prison and the Toulouse central police station, with findings concerning eight transgender women held in those Toulouse facilities. Built on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons, it documents serious persisting violations — isolation imposed for trans status, staff untrained on trans issues, and the 2016 depathologisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) never written into prison rules or healthcare guidance — and recommends financing research, policies against discrimination, and suitable procedures for searching and assigning persons whose civil-status sex does not match their presented identity.

visible.summary: Region research direction: mixed — the country's largest LGBTQ+ community and its biggest police raids coexist, with police acting without legal basis. (1) 1 February 2025: police arrested 56 men at a hotel in the capital at a reported "gay sex party"; organisers risk pornography-law prosecution with penalties up to 15 years; Amnesty International Indonesia called the police's "discriminatory and senseless harassment of LGBTI people ... has no basis in law" and demanded release of those detained. (2) One of the eight provinces where an international NGO found discriminatory regional regulations — and simultaneously the city with the country's densest LGBTQ+ infrastructure, media presence and monitoring-group offices; an assessor should expect both to be true at once. National climate from this record's sources: an October 2025 presidential decree listed "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among the country's non-military national security threats alongside terrorism and drugs, amplifying self-censorship (editors killing LGBTQ+ stories for fear of state reprisal); police deny violence and extortions in the 2022 death-in-custody of a US-based trans activist arrested on drug charges at Bali airport while family members allege he was beaten. Model-estimate residual (route 3, best-knowledge delta): sheer scale of the community limits enforcement reach.
visible.tangentialFactors: The October 2025 national security decree framing LGBTQ+ visibility as a threat shapes the local climate beyond what provincial rules do — journalists and platforms self-censor, reducing the public support infrastructure that gender-nonconforming visitors and residents could otherwise rely on.

sources.claim: Opinion analysis (Aug 2026): an October 2025 presidential decree named "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" a non-military national security threat alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction; journalists report a constant chilling effect (editors killing LGBTQ+ stories fearing state reprisal or religious backlash); civil-society and independent media space has contracted since 2024-25; documented amid student-led anti-government protests.

Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Indonesia' page supplies the national framework the capital stands under and documents Jakarta's raid pattern in detail: police arrested 141 people over a 'gay sex party' in Jakarta in May 2017, detained 144 at the Atlantis Gym sauna on 21 May 2017 (ten charged), and arrested 51 at a Central Jakarta sauna in October 2017 (six charged), all pursued under the pornography law. More recently it records 56 people detained at a hotel in South Jakarta on 1 February 2025, nine detained at another South Jakarta hotel on 24 May 2025, and 75 arrested at a private villa near the capital on 22 June 2025 — offences there can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment. In March 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency declared transgender waria 'socially dysfunctional' and detained trans women in city-run 'rehabilitation' centres unless they signed statements promising not to repeat their 'offence'. Transgender people may change legal gender only after surgery and a judge's approval, and there is no general anti-discrimination law, so police action in Jakarta operates on pornography and morality provisions rather than any LGBT-specific statute.

Amnesty International's 24 June 2025 press release responds to the arrest of 75 people in a raid on a 'gay party' at a privately rented villa in Bogor, near Jakarta, and situates it inside the capital's raid series: 56 people were detained for participating in 'a gay party' at a hotel in South Jakarta on 1 February 2025, and nine were detained following a raid on a different hotel in South Jakarta on 24 May 2025. Amnesty International Indonesia's deputy director called the villa raid 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' that 'exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people in Indonesia', and demanded the release of those arrested. The release notes that police made the arrests without naming detainees or conducting judicial proceedings, and that those detained risk up to 15 years' imprisonment under Indonesia's broadly worded Pornography Law.

visible.summary: Region research direction: worse than national on public-festival access screening — religion-based identity verification doubles as an outing mechanism for gender-nonconforming visitors. After the VHP publicly urged garba (autumn dance festival) organisers not to allow non-Hindus and to check Aadhaar cards for entry, a political row erupted; in Nagpur organisers imposed Aadhaar verification, security checks with "male and female" boundaries and a ritual bow before a Varaha avatar as entry conditions. An identity-checked, religion-screened entry gate at a public festival is precisely the mechanism by which a gender-nonconforming visitor is examined and outed by authorities who are not supposed to be involved — and it is happening in named cities, not nationwide. National backdrop from this record's sources: parliament passed a 2026 amendment bill removing the right to self-identify, limiting recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandating medical certification for gender-affirming procedures, and creating offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender punishable with up to life in prison — prompting nationwide protests from trans communities, with a Supreme Court-appointed panel asking the government to withdraw it; the national census recorded 487,803 transgender persons but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards needed for social security.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2026 national amendment bill strips self-identification, adds anti-"coercion" offences and mandates medical certification — a national climate that raises the cost of being recognised as trans in public in this region as elsewhere, even though it is not region-specific; festival-gate identity screening (this region's own finding) becomes a more acute outing risk under a regime that narrows legal recognition.

sources.claim: National-framework HRW news release, 26 March 2026, on the 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, which the record's national-backdrop paragraph relies on: the bill amends the 2019 law, removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender that HRW calls reminiscent of colonial-era provisions criminalising transgender persons for appearing dressed as women; India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for social security. No Maharashtra-specific content in this source (the record's Nagpur entry-screening claim is not covered here); the article supports the record's claim that this national framework applies in every state including Maharashtra.

National-framework BBC News article on the same 2026 amendment bill: approved by both houses and now needing presidential assent; it removes the right to self-identify, limiting recognition, in a reversal of the 2014 Supreme Court "third gender"/self-determination ruling; critics warn it could exclude many transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people from welfare benefits, and lawyer N Kavitha Rameshwar called the medical-certification requirement an "attack on the privacy and dignity of the individual", while the government argues the narrower definition targets those facing "extreme and oppressive" discrimination and prevents exploitation and trafficking. No Maharashtra-specific content (the record's Nagpur/VHP/Aadhaar festival-screening claim is not covered by this source); the article supports the record's national-backdrop claims.

visible.summary:
Delhi sits at the centre of the country's 2026 reversal on trans rights: parliament passed an amendment bill removing the right to self-identification, restricting legal recognition to traditionally accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandating medical certification, and creating new offences of coercion and allurement punishable up to life imprisonment — a de facto reversal of the 2014 constitutional self-determination ruling, cleared by both houses and awaiting presidential assent. The bill triggered rallies in the capital in March 2026, and a supreme-court-appointed advisory panel urged its withdrawal amid privacy and dignity challenges.

The capital is also where the country's trans population is most institutionally visible: the most recent national census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, of whom roughly 32,500 held identity documents — the documentation gap and the protest politics both concentrate here.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2026 national amendment bill strips self-identification, adds anti-"coercion" offences and mandates medical certification — a national climate that raises the cost of being recognised as trans in public in this capital as elsewhere; under that regime, the capital's own profiling script (transgender read as disguise or illegal migrant) becomes a more acute outing and detention risk than the law alone would imply.

sources.claim: National-framework HRW news release, 26 March 2026 — core source for the record's claims: the 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates "coercing or alluring" offences that could criminalise support systems; HRW calls it a major reversal of hard-won rights and urges the president not to sign it. India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for social security — the national documentation gap the record concentrates in the capital. No Delhi-specific event in this source.

National-framework BBC News article on the 2026 amendment bill: approved by both houses and now awaiting presidential assent; it removes the right to self-identify in a reversal of the 2014 Supreme Court ruling; the record's capital-protest-politics claim is evidenced here — activist Grace Banu told a press conference in Delhi the community sought "recognition without invasion" and "rights without humiliation" — and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel has asked the government to reconsider amid privacy-and-dignity challenges. The government argues the narrower definition will make welfare benefits, job reservations and healthcare support more targeted while strengthening protections against exploitation and trafficking.

visible.summary:
This state is where the country's religious-enforcement apparatus has been most visibly exercised against gender expression: in 2021 its religious department issued an arrest warrant for a prominent transgender businesswoman over her presentation and mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers in a manhunt that preceded her leaving the country, an episode documented in international analysis of state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia.

The national framework applies unchanged here: same-sex conduct is criminalised with sentences up to 20 years and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and the day-to-day exposure for gender-nonconforming visitors runs precisely through this state's religious-offence enforcement.
visible.tangentialFactors: Anti-Pride hostility at the state level — the January 2026 probe into a 'Glamping with Pride' gathering and the official 'no LGBT promotion' stance — targets queer visibility generally and spills over onto trans visitors in the state's tourism corridor.

sources.claim: Malaysia country profile (Human Dignity Trust, last updated 16 December 2025) with both the national framework and Selangor-specific enforcement: Penal Code sections 377A-377D criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment with whipping (a law enforced in recent years; both men and women, and usable against trans people), and Sharia state enactments criminalise cross-dressing and "males posing as females"; Selangor-specific content — the Federal Court struck down provisions of Selangor's Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding state power (2021), the Selangor state authorities issued an arrest warrant for a trans businesswoman who failed to appear in court and announced the deployment of 122 religious-affairs officers (the Sajat case), and a Selangor Sharia court sentenced five men to six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane; at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown on the LGBT community ongoing since the 2018 election.

HRW/Justice for Sisters report release (10 August 2022) documenting Malaysia's state-backed discrimination, including the Selangor episode the record leads with: in 2021 Nur Sajat, a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur, failed to appear in court in Selangor to answer criminal charges for "insulting Islam" based on her attire; the state's religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from Thailand — a deployment HRW/JFS cite as showing how far authorities go to enforce rigid gender norms (she was permitted to stay under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia). National framework context: the federal penal code punishes oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison, Sharia codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, investigations covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, and state "rehabilitation" programmes were found to internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred.
